'''Aaron Patrick Titus''' (born April 6, 1971) is an American professor of [[physics]] at [[North Carolina State University]] (NCSU), and co-founder of the online learning and homework service [[WebAssign]]. Titus has won multiple teaching awards for his work in [[tertiary education]].

Born in [[Wenatchee, Washington]], he received his B.S. in physics from [[Penn State University]] in 1993, married his wife Kimberly Jo Titus ({{nee|Gossett}}) in 1994, and completed his Ph.D. in physics from NCSU in 1998. A year prior, Titus collaborated with [[North Park University]] professor Larry Martin to merge each of their respective online learning and homework services together to create WebAssign. Titus then began to teach at [[North Carolina A&T State University]] from 1998 to 2002, then at [[High Point University]] (HPU) until 2022, and has taught at NCSU since. Titus has started multiple sponsored projects aimed at improving education in targeted areas. At HPU in particular, Titus played a key role in establishing the university's physics major and Department of Physics, serving as the new department's first [[Chair (academic department)|chair]]. Titus also co-authored the 5th edition of the introductory calculus-based physics textbook ''Matter and Interactions'', after contributing to the two preceding editions.

Titus received the Meredith Clark Slane Distinguished Teaching Service Award in 2011, the highest teaching distinction at HPU, and the Excellence in Physics Education Award of the [[American Physical Society]] in 2019, shared with an eighteen-member Open Source Physics Team.

== Career ==
=== WebAssign ===
{{main|WebAssign}}
{{Quote box
 |quote   = In the past, when professors were hand-grading everything, that was the biggest time constraint. And by the time students got homework back, they might not even remember why they got an answer wrong.
 |author  = — Aaron Titus
 |source  = in an interview with ''AUTM''<ref name="AUTM"/>
 |width   = 25%
 |align   = right
 |bgcolor = #F0FFF0
 |quoted  = yes
}}
While studying for his Ph.D. at NCSU in the 1990s, Titus worked as a [[teaching assistant]] for physics professor John Risley, who shared Titus's vision for incorporating technology into education.<ref name="AUTM">{{cite web |title=Delivering Instant Feedback for Math and Science Students for Instructors and Students |url=https://autm.net/about-tech-transfer/better-world-project/bwp-stories/webassign-ubiquitous-online-instructional-tools-fo |work=AUTM |access-date=August 29, 2025 |archive-date=March 5, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260305112414/https://autm.net/about-tech-transfer/better-world-project/bwp-stories/webassign-ubiquitous-online-instructional-tools-fo |url-status=live}}</ref> In relation to this, Titus created an online learning and homework service named "PhysWeb" in 1996, a service which included animated demonstrations for solving problems.<ref name="MICDS"/> The service, however, only worked with multiple choice questions.<ref name="AUTM"/> In the summer of 1996, Titus showcased the service at an [[American Association of Physics Teachers]] (AAPT) meeting.<ref name="MS2017"/> After the presentation, Titus spoke with a visiting professor from [[North Park University]] in [[Chicago, Illinois]], named Larry Martin, who had created an online learning and homework service of his own called "WWWAssign".<ref name="MS2017"/><ref name="MICDS"/><ref name="Thompson">{{cite web |last1=Thompson |first1=Scott |title=Risleys establish endowed physics professorship |url=https://sciences.ncsu.edu/news/risleys-establish-endowed-physics-professorship/ |work=North Carolina State University College of Sciences News |date=May 20, 2011 |access-date=August 29, 2025 |archive-date=December 8, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151208175552/https://sciences.ncsu.edu/news/risleys-establish-endowed-physics-professorship/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Martin's service notably generated random numbers for homework questions, allowing students to work together on similar problems, but requiring them to calculate an answer with their own numbers to submit.<ref name="AUTM"/> With both services offering features the other lacked, NCSU recruited Martin for a two-year [[sabbatical]] to work with Titus to create a combined service.<ref name="MICDS"/><ref name="AUTM"/> With the project supervised by Professor Risley, Titus's database structure and Martin's code were combined to co-create the first version of [[WebAssign]] in the autumn of 1997.<ref name="MICDS"/><ref name="AUTM"/> The combined service produced randomized numbers in questions, and allowed students to view upcoming due dates for homework, gain immediate feedback on answers, and access online tutorials for help with problems: features not previously possible through paper homework.<ref name="AUTM"/> Despite only featuring about 1,000 questions total at the time of launch, a number of STEM professors at NCSU adopted the service.<ref name="AUTM"/> Early feedback from professors who pioneered the service helped Titus and Martin find and fix [[software bug]]s, including one that allowed infinite submission attempts on questions without penalty.<ref name="AUTM"/>

In 1998, WebAssign was made commercially available to use outside NCSU.<ref name="AUTM"/> In 2002, an academic paper authored by Titus and fellow academic Guo-Qing Tang concluded that WebAssign increased interaction in the classroom. Additionally, the service was found to aid students in their completion of homework outside of the classroom, and instructors in their ability to create assignments based on student feedback.<ref name="Serhan">{{cite journal |last1=Serhan |first1=Derar |title=Web-Based Homework Systems: Students' Perceptions of Course Interaction and Learning in Mathematics |url=https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1264260.pdf |journal=International Journal on Social and Education Sciences |issn=2688-7061 |volume=1 |issue=2 |page=57 |year=2019 |access-date=August 27, 2025 |archive-date=February 2, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250202035345/http://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1264260.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Valdez">{{cite web |last1=Valdez |first1=Ma. Theresa Christine C. |last2=Maderal |first2=Lea D. |title=An Analysis of Students' Perception of Online Assessments and its Relation to Motivation Towards Mathematics Learning |url=https://academic-publishing.org/index.php/ejel/article/view/2481/2001 |journal=Electronic Journal of e-Learning |volume=19 |number=5 |issn=1479-4403 |page=428 |year=2021 |access-date=August 27, 2025 |archive-date=November 13, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241113205210/https://academic-publishing.org/index.php/ejel/article/view/2481/2001 |url-status=live}}</ref> The service remained under NCSU until 2003, when the copyright for some of the service's software code was transferred to its own company named Advanced Instructional Systems Inc., which was headed by Risley as [[CEO]].<ref name="AUTM"/> Since its launch as an independent company the service has expanded and reached a wider audience.<ref name="AUTM"/><ref name="Thompson"/> By 2011, the service was used by 500,000 students across 1,500 institutions worldwide.<ref name="Thompson"/> In 2023, the [[Mary Institute and St. Louis Country Day School]] referred to the service as the "number one homework system used for calculus".<ref name="MICDS"/>

== Awards and recognition ==
Titus has received awards from the physics societies AAPT and the [[American Physical Society]] (APS). The AAPT awarded him the "Best [[Pedagogical]] Paper" twice, in 2001 and 2011,<ref name="ElectBio">{{cite web |last1=Titus |first1=Aaron |title=AAron Titus 2012 Election Bio: Aaron Titus |url=https://www.aapt.org/aboutaapt/organization/titus_2012_election_bio.cfm |publisher=[[American Association of Physics Teachers]] |year=2012 |access-date=August 29, 2025 |archive-date=March 17, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260317123615/https://aapt.org/aboutaapt/organization/titus_2012_election_bio.cfm |url-status=live}}</ref> the "[[Homer L. Dodge]] Citation for Distinguished Service" for exceptional contributions to the association in 2019,<ref name="HLDC"/><ref name="MA"/> and the "[[David Halliday (physicist)|David Halliday]] and [[Robert Resnick]] Award" for exceptional teaching of undergraduate physics in 2026.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Antelis |first1=Miriam |title=Physicist Titus Honored for Excellence in Undergraduate Physics |url=https://sciences.ncsu.edu/news/physicist-titus-honored-for-excellence-in-undergraduate-physics/ |work=North Carolina State University College of Sciences News |date=March 20, 2026 |access-date=June 4, 2026 |archive-date=June 4, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260604234015/https://sciences.ncsu.edu/news/physicist-titus-honored-for-excellence-in-undergraduate-physics/ |url-status=live}}</ref> In 2019, Titus was one of eighteen members of the Open Source Physics Team which won the "2020 Excellence in Physics Education Award" from the APS for continued commitment to computational physics education.<ref name="MICDS"/><ref>{{cite press release |title=Spring 2020 American Physical Society Prizes and Awards Announced |url=https://www.aps.org/about/news/2019/10/spring-2020-aps-prizes-announced |publisher=[[American Physical Society]] |date=October 22, 2019 |access-date=August 29, 2025 |archive-date=June 18, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250618202420/https://www.aps.org/about/news/2019/10/spring-2020-aps-prizes-announced |url-status=live}}</ref>

Titus has also received awards from schools he's taught at, namely HPU and NCSU. He received the "Evening Degree Program Outstanding Faculty Member" award from HPU in 2009,<ref name="ElectBio"/> and the "Meredith Clark Slane Distinguished Teaching-Service Award" from HPU in 2011 in recognition of teaching excellence,<ref name="REIT">{{cite news |title=Recognizing Excellence: Innovative Teaching Inspires Student Achievement |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/960835105/ |work=[[News & Record]] |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |location=[[Greensboro, North Carolina]] |page=3 |date=October 9, 2011 |access-date=August 29, 2025 |url-access=limited |archive-date=September 9, 2025
